blocks.title: Clustering
blocks.text: Clustering groups similar things together by their characteristics. K-means is one of the simplest and most popular methods: we choose the number of groups, K, and the algorithm groups points by their distance from cluster centres.

items: Choose K = 2: one cluster for students stronger in Math, one for students stronger in English.
Place initial centres: Basim (85, 70) and Tallat (40, 85).

Assign each student to the nearest centre using Euclidean distance. Umer is 7.1 from Basim; Anie is 11.2 from Tallat; Maliha is 26.9 from Basim and 32.0 from Tallat, so she joins Basim. Cluster 1 is Basim, Umer, Maliha; cluster 2 is Anie, Tallat.
Recalculate each centre as the average of its members: cluster 1 (78.3, 65), cluster 2 (45, 82.5).
Repeat assigning and recalculating until the centres stop moving. Here nobody changes cluster, so the result is stable.

blocks.text: Euclidean distance between (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is the square root of (x1 - x2)^2 + (y1 - y2)^2; for Maliha and Basim it is the square root of 25^2 + 10^2 = 725, about 26.9.

blocks.alt: Top left: five points of customers against earnings on the line earnings = 100 + 40 x customers, with a prediction of Rs 980 for 22 customers and an actual day-6 point of 1,250. Top right: an S-shaped probability curve over pass/fail points for 1 to 6 hours of study. Bottom left: Math and English scores of five students in two K-means clusters with centres marked x. Bottom right: five model-building steps.
blocks.caption: Linear regression, logistic regression and K-means (original diagram after topic 5.4).
blocks.long_description: The fruit-stall data lie exactly on the line earnings = 100 + 40 x customers, so 22 customers predict 980 rupees, and on day 6 the model predicted 1,220 for 28 customers against an actual 1,250. A logistic model turns study hours into a probability of passing that rises in an S-shape from near 0 to near 1, crossing 0.5 between the failing and passing students; the curve drawn is illustrative. K-means with K = 2 groups Basim, Umer and Maliha around a centre at Math 78.3, English 65, and Anie and Tallat around Math 45, English 82.5. A model is built by defining the problem, collecting data, choosing an algorithm, training and evaluating on new data.

blocks.prompt: What is the primary goal of K-means (MCQ 8)? What does K represent (MCQ 9)? Explain the algorithm step by step (long question 5).
blocks.explanation: (b) to group data into clusters by similarity; (b) the number of clusters. Steps: choose K; pick K initial centroids, often K data points chosen at random (here Basim and Tallat); assign every point to its nearest centroid by Euclidean distance; move each centroid to the mean of its assigned points; repeat assignment and update until the centroids stop changing. The final clusters are the groups of similar points.

items: K-means (K = 2): Basim, Umer, Maliha around (78.3, 65); Anie, Tallat around (45, 82.5).
